 How We Tested
 Since 2011, we have researched, purchased, and tested dozens of portable solar panels for camping. Our rigorous side-by-side tests pit these sun-gathering machines against each other. Much of our testing involved measuring how quickly each solar panel charged a battery at the same location and time to ensure the most accurate results. We connected each solar panel to a matching battery simultaneously to ensure identical conditions, then recorded the charge each panel generated in two hours. 
 Our testing of these solar panels is divided into three rating metrics with weights corresponding to their overall importance: 
 Power Efficiency (60% of overall weighting) 
 Portability (20% of overall weighting) 
 Ease of Setup (20% of overall weighting) 
 Why Trust GearLab
 Our expert panel review team is led by Kenji Mowrey . Kenji has been a Review Editor at GearLab for three years. He tests power stations for Gear Lab, so it only makes sense to have him lead the testing for solar panels as well. Kenji is passionate about running, biking, and camping. He holds a bachelor's degree in Outdoor Product Design from Oregon State and draws on his camping experience and knack for design to understand what makes a great solar panel. 
 Sam Schild also lent his expertise and writing abilities in putting together this review. Sam is an avid outdoorsy person who has spent countless nights camping miles away from the nearest electrical outlet. He first used a solar panel during a cross-country bicycle tour in 2012 to power his cell phone. He currently lives full-time in a campervan with 300 watts of solar panels attached to the roof for power.

 What's the Best Value?
 Price doesn't always equal performance in this category. Several of the most expensive panels we tested underperformed in efficiency and other key areas. Some of our top-rated panels were also among the best values. Keep in mind that price per watt depends on current sales. For the best energy output per dollar, divide the lowest price you can find by our “ Measured Watts ” (listed below in the review text and above in the specs).
 The Renogy 200W Portable is our top overall pick and offers the best value among the portable solar panels we tested for camping and off-grid use. If it had not won Editors' Choice, it would have won Best Buy. While not the cheapest option, it delivers consistently excellent performance and efficiency. And it costs hundreds less than many other models. 
 It's worth paying a few extra bucks for the Renogy 200W Portable panel because it's efficient and very portable.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W is one of the least expensive panels we tested that still works well. This panel doesn't fold, so it isn't the best for every use case, but if you're looking for an inexpensive panel to mount on your roof, whether that's a moving or fixed roof, this is a great option that won't break the bank. We have also seen some RV users buy inexpensive generic stands for using this panel on the ground. It is heavier and bulkier than the foldable options in this review, but with the right support, it can be made pretty sturdy and wind-resistant.
 The FlexSolar 100W costs less than every other panel in this review. But this model is only 100 watts, whereas most of the other panels here are 200 watts. So while the FlexSolar is the least expensive, it isn't the least expensive per watt —that award goes to the JJn Bifacial 200W . 
 In the chart below, we show the cost per watt for each panel. We calculate this by dividing the price by the actual efficiency we measured in testing, rather than the manufacturer's claimed rating.
 The Marbero 200W Portable is also very inexpensive, making it a great value for a folding 200-watt solar panel. However, this panel's measured watt output is only 134 watts. So, the cost per watt of this panel is $1.32, which is more than the JJN and the FlexSolar . You may be paying less for this panel, but you are also getting less power than expected.
 You'll pay a low cost per watt for the JJN Bifacial 200W, and we're talking measured watts here.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W produced the most raw output of any panel in our lineup at 193 measured watts. This panel regularly sells for 40-50% off MSRP, and this “ street price ” is a great value. 
 We've never actually seen the EcoFlow NextGen 220W sold for its MSRP, so be sure to buy this one when it's discounted.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the best value for van lifers and overlanders who want to mount a panel on top of their rig. It's one of the lightest panels we tested, is pretty efficient overall, and only requires industrial adhesive or double-stick tape to mount—no drilling or extra hardware required. This saves you money and time. 
 Power Efficiency
 The main use of a large solar panel is to convert sunlight into energy, so we weighted this metric heavily. If a panel doesn't reliably generate power, then it isn't worth the investment, no matter how portable or easy to set up it might be. 
 We used two measured results to assess power efficiency: the number of watts charged in 2 hours of direct sunlight, and the percent of the claimed power (in watts) actually delivered when charging a power station. A 100% efficient system using a 200-watt panel would charge 200 watt-hours in each hour of direct sun, but how efficient is each of these systems?
 We connected each panel to an identical Jackery portable power station to test charging capabilities.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 To test power efficiency, we connected each panel to a Jackery 1000 power station (1070Wh capacity). We then let the panels charge their respective battery for two hours and calculated the total watt-hours generated. During the test, we recorded the input power every 30 minutes to calculate the actual output power relative to each panel's claimed wattage. 
 We performed these power-efficiency tests at an elevation of 6300 feet on a clear day. The temperature was between 55 and 65° F.
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W generated the most charge over our two-hour test. This panel generated 385 watts over the test period, for a measured power of 193 watts per hour. If this panel were 200 watts like most of the rest of the test lineup, that would be extremely efficient. As it is, though, this panel remains very efficient and generated the most power during our tests. If you're going by looks, this panel is about the same size as the other folding models, though. So the fact that it's technically less efficient because it's 20 watts more than the competition is kind of a moot point. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is technically a 220-watt panel, while most of the other models we tested are 200 watts.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W generated 182 watts per hour, charging its 1070-watt-hour test battery a whopping 34% in two hours. Input readings were consistently between 194 and 200 watts throughout our two-hour test. Its bifacial cell design, which captures light on both sides of the panel, almost certainly contributes to this exceptional performance. And 182 watts in an hour is 91% of the 200 watts this panel is rated for. That's super efficient. 
 If you needed to fully charge a 1000-watt-hour battery, which is a common size for a power station, you could do that with either the EcoFlow NextGen or the JJN Bifacial in about 6 hours. That's some serious power. 
 The next most efficient solar panel is the Renogy 200W Portable . This panel generated 177 watts in an hour. You could also theoretically charge a 1000-watt-hour battery from 0 to 100% in about 6 hours with this model. And since it's a 200W panel, its measured efficiency is higher than the EcoFlow NextGen 's, too. 
 Just behind those panels is the Jackery SolarSaga 200 . This panel produced 171 watts per hour at 86% efficiency. This is one of the most consistent foldable panels in our test lineup.
 Elevation, air temperature, and the surface you set your panel on can all affect a solar panel's energy output. We've found that hotter weather and lower elevations reduce solar panel efficiency. Laying your panel directly on a hot surface, such as blacktop or the roof of your house, will reduce efficiency, especially if the battery is also on that same surface. Instead, prop your panel up on its kickstand legs to create airflow below, which will keep it cooler and boost efficiency. 
 The next highest-scoring panels in power efficiency were the BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible , Anker Solix PS200 , and Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase . Each of these panels charged its test battery to 31% in two hours.
 The Anker Solix charged our test battery almost as efficiently as the top-performing panels.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Portability
 While not as important as power efficiency, portability is also a consideration when choosing a solar panel. 
 We tested portability by weighing each model with a scale in our test lab. We also measured the size of each panel when folded and when opened. Most of the models we tested here are designed to be packed into your trunk and set up wherever you need them. So, we also assessed how easy it was to transport these panels throughout the test period. We paid special attention to features that made carrying them easier, such as ergonomic handles, cable storage, and carrying cases. 
 Most of the panels we tested have carrying handles, which made weighing them on our test lab's luggage scale a cinch.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The easiest panel to carry is the FlexSolar 100W . This panel weighs only 4.1 pounds and folds down to the size of a laptop. Most of the other panels we tested are 200 watts, and more surface area is required for more watts. But even the 100-watt versions of these other panels are still larger and heavier than the FlexSolar 100W. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the lightest 200-watt panel we tested. This model only weighs 6.6 pounds. That's over twice as light as the next most portable 200-watt model. 
 The Arch doesn't fold, though, and doesn't have carrying handles or a place to stash cables. It's designed to be mounted on a fiberglass van roof, a boat, a hardshell rooftop tent, or another surface without weighing it down. So even though this panel is significantly lighter than most folding models, we wouldn't necessarily choose it for a panel to pack in the trunk with your camping gear.
 The lightest foldable 200-watt panels are the Jackery SolarSaga 200 (14.2 lbs), Marbero 200W Portable (14.2 lbs), and Renogy 200W Portable (14.8 lbs). These panels fold down to a smaller size than the BougeRV Arch . And even though they weigh over twice as much, they're easier to carry and pack in a trunk because they have a handle and fold. 
 The Renogy 200W Portable has a zippered pocket large enough to store a phone or small accessories along with the integrated charging cables. This makes it easier to pack and stay organized, despite the extra half-pound of weight compared to the Marbero and Jackery. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is one of the few folding panels with a separate carrying case, which you may or may not prefer.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W weighs 16.5 lbs and comes with a carrying case to protect the panel during transport. This is useful, but if you lose the case, the panel becomes much harder to carry. For this reason, we prefer built-in handles to a separate case. But you might feel differently. 
 The Anker Solix PS200 (17.1 lbs) and Grecell 200W Portable (17.3 lbs) are comparable in terms of portability. The Anker uses snap buttons to keep it folded up during transport. The Grecell has a cable storage bag and two clips to prevent it from unfolding. 
 The ZOUPW 200W Foldable (18.3 lbs) and Bluetti 200W Portable (18.9 lbs) are on the heavier side for folding 200W panels. You can still carry either of these on your own, but the extra weight is noticeable compared to the lighter models listed above.
 Technically, the Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase is portable, but you won't want to carry it far.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase , at 43.3 lbs, is the least portable panel we tested. The fact that it has a carrying handle and a carrying case is helpful in some ways, but many people will still find it too heavy to carry on their own. We'd prefer to have a friend help carry it, and it's much easier to fit it into the carrying bag with help, too. This panel is best for setting up in a location and leaving it there, so the fact that it even has a handle feels wrong. 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W , on the other hand, doesn't try to be portable. At 25 lbs, this panel weighs significantly less than the Goal Zero Briefcase. But it doesn't fold or have a carrying handle. This is also better for setting up in a location and not moving it ever again, unless it's attached to the roof of a vehicle. 
 By measuring both weight and ease of transport, we arrived at our overall portability score.
 We wouldn't recommend loading the JJN Bifacial into the trunk of your car as we did.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Ease of Setup
 A portable solar panel that is hard to set up defeats the purpose of it being portable. When you're camping, you don't want to spend hours setting up solar panels; you want to enjoy nature, right?
 We evaluated ease of setup by timing how long it took us to set up each panel. Setup time for each panel varied widely — it ranged from 31 seconds to 10 minutes! 
 We also used qualitative ratings based on what makes it easier or harder to start charging with these panels. We looked at how the kickstand legs worked, how much you could adjust the angle, built-in cable storage options, wind stability, and more. 
 The amount of time it takes to set up a portable solar panel controls how quickly you can relax at camp.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Renogy 200W Portable was the easiest to set up overall. It sets up in just 35 seconds, so you can start charging shortly after getting to camp. And once you've set this panel up, it's sturdier than other portable solar panels. While its kickstand legs look similar to those of other budget folding panels, they are larger and sturdier. This panel is more wind-resistant than other folding models we tested, especially when you use stakes to secure the legs. It also has a zippered pouch for storing cables when you're not using them, which keeps things much tidier in a packed trunk. 
 The Jackery SolarSaga 200 is also very easy to set up. We had this panel upright and charging in 35 seconds. It has kickstand legs that deploy quickly, and the magnetic closure on the handle opens easily when you want it to, not when you don't. The charging cable has an 8 mm DC connector, which pairs perfectly with the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 models we used for testing. If you're trying to use this panel with a different power station brand, you'll likely need to buy a common adaptor. Some panels come with several adaptors so they can easily attach to any power station battery, but not this one. 
 The Grecell 200W Portable went from folded to charging in 31 seconds, the shortest time of any model. This panel also comes with MC4 power cables with four different connector types, so it can connect to any power station without requiring you to purchase the correct adaptor. However, after the testing period, the stitching on the canvas covering the panel is already beginning to separate. This makes us skeptical about how long it will last. 
 The Goal Zero Boulder Briefcase took longer to set up than most of the other folding panels we tested.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Anker Solix PS200 set up in 43 seconds, which is still quite fast, albeit not quite the fastest. But this panel has tons of other useful features. The kickstand legs have snap buttons to adjust the angle. Each leg has four different attachment points at 30, 40, 50, and 80 degrees. Since the legs are on the longer side, it takes a bit of maneuvering to keep them spread out when setting up with one person. But this also makes the panel more stable once you've set it up. It has MC4 connector cables, but they're shorter than most other panels. For long-term use, we recommend getting an extension cable.
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible and JJN Bifacial 200W are also notable in this category. They take much longer to set up than the folding models. The BougeRV takes 400 seconds, and the JJN 600 seconds. However, neither of these panels needs to be taken down once you've attached them to the roof of your vehicle, so technically the setup time is zero seconds after the initial setup. But, mounting these panels requires some hardware and mechanical know-how. So if you aren't looking to install a panel on your vehicle's roof, you should opt for a folding, portable solar panel. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible requires no setup time once you've mounted it to the roof of your vehicle.   Credit: Sam Schild 
 Conclusion
 Choosing the right portable solar panel for your camping setup can feel daunting. Making the correct purchase can be the difference between a panel that lasts a long time and one that leaves you short on charge in the backcountry. Now that we've given you our take on the best large solar panels, hopefully you can make the right purchasing decision for your needs. 
 Hopefully, this guide brings you to beautiful places with plenty of power for all your tech.   Credit: Sam Schild

 How We Tested
 Since 2011, we have researched, purchased, and tested dozens of portable solar panels for camping. Our rigorous side-by-side tests pit these sun-gathering machines against each other. Much of our testing involved measuring how quickly each solar panel charged a battery at the same location and time to ensure the most accurate results. We connected each solar panel to a matching battery simultaneously to ensure identical conditions, then recorded the charge each panel generated in two hours. 
 Our testing of these solar panels is divided into three rating metrics with weights corresponding to their overall importance: 
 Power Efficiency (60% of overall weighting) 
 Portability (20% of overall weighting) 
 Ease of Setup (20% of overall weighting) 
 Why Trust GearLab
 Our expert panel review team is led by Kenji Mowrey . Kenji has been a Review Editor at GearLab for three years. He tests power stations for Gear Lab, so it only makes sense to have him lead the testing for solar panels as well. Kenji is passionate about running, biking, and camping. He holds a bachelor's degree in Outdoor Product Design from Oregon State and draws on his camping experience and knack for design to understand what makes a great solar panel. 
 Sam Schild also lent his expertise and writing abilities in putting together this review. Sam is an avid outdoorsy person who has spent countless nights camping miles away from the nearest electrical outlet. He first used a solar panel during a cross-country bicycle tour in 2012 to power his cell phone. He currently lives full-time in a campervan with 300 watts of solar panels attached to the roof for power. 
 Previous Next 
 We tested these panels side-by-side to ensure consistent conditions and get reliable results.
 Analysis and Test Results
 Worse Value
 Better Value
 What's the Best Value?
 Price doesn't always equal performance in this category. Several of the most expensive panels we tested underperformed in efficiency and other key areas. Some of our top-rated panels were also among the best values. Keep in mind that price per watt depends on current sales. For the best energy output per dollar, divide the lowest price you can find by our “ Measured Watts ” (listed below in the review text and above in the specs).
 The Renogy 200W Portable is our top overall pick and offers the best value among the portable solar panels we tested for camping and off-grid use. If it had not won Editors' Choice, it would have won Best Buy. While not the cheapest option, it delivers consistently excellent performance and efficiency. And it costs hundreds less than many other models. 
 It's worth paying a few extra bucks for the Renogy 200W Portable panel because it's efficient and very portable.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W is one of the least expensive panels we tested that still works well. This panel doesn't fold, so it isn't the best for every use case, but if you're looking for an inexpensive panel to mount on your roof, whether that's a moving or fixed roof, this is a great option that won't break the bank. We have also seen some RV users buy inexpensive generic stands for using this panel on the ground. It is heavier and bulkier than the foldable options in this review, but with the right support, it can be made pretty sturdy and wind-resistant.
 The FlexSolar 100W costs less than every other panel in this review. But this model is only 100 watts, whereas most of the other panels here are 200 watts. So while the FlexSolar is the least expensive, it isn't the least expensive per watt —that award goes to the JJn Bifacial 200W . 
 In the chart below, we show the cost per watt for each panel. We calculate this by dividing the price by the actual efficiency we measured in testing, rather than the manufacturer's claimed rating.
 The Marbero 200W Portable is also very inexpensive, making it a great value for a folding 200-watt solar panel. However, this panel's measured watt output is only 134 watts. So, the cost per watt of this panel is $1.32, which is more than the JJN and the FlexSolar . You may be paying less for this panel, but you are also getting less power than expected.
 You'll pay a low cost per watt for the JJN Bifacial 200W, and we're talking measured watts here.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W produced the most raw output of any panel in our lineup at 193 measured watts. This panel regularly sells for 40-50% off MSRP, and this “ street price ” is a great value. 
 We've never actually seen the EcoFlow NextGen 220W sold for its MSRP, so be sure to buy this one when it's discounted.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the best value for van lifers and overlanders who want to mount a panel on top of their rig. It's one of the lightest panels we tested, is pretty efficient overall, and only requires industrial adhesive or double-stick tape to mount—no drilling or extra hardware required. This saves you money and time. 
 Power Efficiency
 The main use of a large solar panel is to convert sunlight into energy, so we weighted this metric heavily. If a panel doesn't reliably generate power, then it isn't worth the investment, no matter how portable or easy to set up it might be. 
 We used two measured results to assess power efficiency: the number of watts charged in 2 hours of direct sunlight, and the percent of the claimed power (in watts) actually delivered when charging a power station. A 100% efficient system using a 200-watt panel would charge 200 watt-hours in each hour of direct sun, but how efficient is each of these systems?
 We connected each panel to an identical Jackery portable power station to test charging capabilities.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 To test power efficiency, we connected each panel to a Jackery 1000 power station (1070Wh capacity). We then let the panels charge their respective battery for two hours and calculated the total watt-hours generated. During the test, we recorded the input power every 30 minutes to calculate the actual output power relative to each panel's claimed wattage. 
 We performed these power-efficiency tests at an elevation of 6300 feet on a clear day. The temperature was between 55 and 65° F.
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W generated the most charge over our two-hour test. This panel generated 385 watts over the test period, for a measured power of 193 watts per hour. If this panel were 200 watts like most of the rest of the test lineup, that would be extremely efficient. As it is, though, this panel remains very efficient and generated the most power during our tests. If you're going by looks, this panel is about the same size as the other folding models, though. So the fact that it's technically less efficient because it's 20 watts more than the competition is kind of a moot point. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is technically a 220-watt panel, while most of the other models we tested are 200 watts.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W generated 182 watts per hour, charging its 1070-watt-hour test battery a whopping 34% in two hours. Input readings were consistently between 194 and 200 watts throughout our two-hour test. Its bifacial cell design, which captures light on both sides of the panel, almost certainly contributes to this exceptional performance. And 182 watts in an hour is 91% of the 200 watts this panel is rated for. That's super efficient. 
 If you needed to fully charge a 1000-watt-hour battery, which is a common size for a power station, you could do that with either the EcoFlow NextGen or the JJN Bifacial in about 6 hours. That's some serious power. 
 The next most efficient solar panel is the Renogy 200W Portable . This panel generated 177 watts in an hour. You could also theoretically charge a 1000-watt-hour battery from 0 to 100% in about 6 hours with this model. And since it's a 200W panel, its measured efficiency is higher than the EcoFlow NextGen 's, too. 
 Just behind those panels is the Jackery SolarSaga 200 . This panel produced 171 watts per hour at 86% efficiency. This is one of the most consistent foldable panels in our test lineup.
 Elevation, air temperature, and the surface you set your panel on can all affect a solar panel's energy output. We've found that hotter weather and lower elevations reduce solar panel efficiency. Laying your panel directly on a hot surface, such as blacktop or the roof of your house, will reduce efficiency, especially if the battery is also on that same surface. Instead, prop your panel up on its kickstand legs to create airflow below, which will keep it cooler and boost efficiency. 
 The next highest-scoring panels in power efficiency were the BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible , Anker Solix PS200 , and Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase . Each of these panels charged its test battery to 31% in two hours.
 The Anker Solix charged our test battery almost as efficiently as the top-performing panels.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Portability
 While not as important as power efficiency, portability is also a consideration when choosing a solar panel. 
 We tested portability by weighing each model with a scale in our test lab. We also measured the size of each panel when folded and when opened. Most of the models we tested here are designed to be packed into your trunk and set up wherever you need them. So, we also assessed how easy it was to transport these panels throughout the test period. We paid special attention to features that made carrying them easier, such as ergonomic handles, cable storage, and carrying cases. 
 Most of the panels we tested have carrying handles, which made weighing them on our test lab's luggage scale a cinch.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The easiest panel to carry is the FlexSolar 100W . This panel weighs only 4.1 pounds and folds down to the size of a laptop. Most of the other panels we tested are 200 watts, and more surface area is required for more watts. But even the 100-watt versions of these other panels are still larger and heavier than the FlexSolar 100W. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible is the lightest 200-watt panel we tested. This model only weighs 6.6 pounds. That's over twice as light as the next most portable 200-watt model. 
 The Arch doesn't fold, though, and doesn't have carrying handles or a place to stash cables. It's designed to be mounted on a fiberglass van roof, a boat, a hardshell rooftop tent, or another surface without weighing it down. So even though this panel is significantly lighter than most folding models, we wouldn't necessarily choose it for a panel to pack in the trunk with your camping gear.
 The lightest foldable 200-watt panels are the Jackery SolarSaga 200 (14.2 lbs), Marbero 200W Portable (14.2 lbs), and Renogy 200W Portable (14.8 lbs). These panels fold down to a smaller size than the BougeRV Arch . And even though they weigh over twice as much, they're easier to carry and pack in a trunk because they have a handle and fold. 
 The Renogy 200W Portable has a zippered pocket large enough to store a phone or small accessories along with the integrated charging cables. This makes it easier to pack and stay organized, despite the extra half-pound of weight compared to the Marbero and Jackery. 
 The EcoFlow NextGen is one of the few folding panels with a separate carrying case, which you may or may not prefer.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The EcoFlow NextGen 220W weighs 16.5 lbs and comes with a carrying case to protect the panel during transport. This is useful, but if you lose the case, the panel becomes much harder to carry. For this reason, we prefer built-in handles to a separate case. But you might feel differently. 
 The Anker Solix PS200 (17.1 lbs) and Grecell 200W Portable (17.3 lbs) are comparable in terms of portability. The Anker uses snap buttons to keep it folded up during transport. The Grecell has a cable storage bag and two clips to prevent it from unfolding. 
 The ZOUPW 200W Foldable (18.3 lbs) and Bluetti 200W Portable (18.9 lbs) are on the heavier side for folding 200W panels. You can still carry either of these on your own, but the extra weight is noticeable compared to the lighter models listed above.
 Technically, the Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase is portable, but you won't want to carry it far.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Goal Zero Boulder 200 Briefcase , at 43.3 lbs, is the least portable panel we tested. The fact that it has a carrying handle and a carrying case is helpful in some ways, but many people will still find it too heavy to carry on their own. We'd prefer to have a friend help carry it, and it's much easier to fit it into the carrying bag with help, too. This panel is best for setting up in a location and leaving it there, so the fact that it even has a handle feels wrong. 
 The JJN Bifacial 200W , on the other hand, doesn't try to be portable. At 25 lbs, this panel weighs significantly less than the Goal Zero Briefcase. But it doesn't fold or have a carrying handle. This is also better for setting up in a location and not moving it ever again, unless it's attached to the roof of a vehicle. 
 By measuring both weight and ease of transport, we arrived at our overall portability score.
 We wouldn't recommend loading the JJN Bifacial into the trunk of your car as we did.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 Ease of Setup
 A portable solar panel that is hard to set up defeats the purpose of it being portable. When you're camping, you don't want to spend hours setting up solar panels; you want to enjoy nature, right?
 We evaluated ease of setup by timing how long it took us to set up each panel. Setup time for each panel varied widely — it ranged from 31 seconds to 10 minutes! 
 We also used qualitative ratings based on what makes it easier or harder to start charging with these panels. We looked at how the kickstand legs worked, how much you could adjust the angle, built-in cable storage options, wind stability, and more. 
 The amount of time it takes to set up a portable solar panel controls how quickly you can relax at camp.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Renogy 200W Portable was the easiest to set up overall. It sets up in just 35 seconds, so you can start charging shortly after getting to camp. And once you've set this panel up, it's sturdier than other portable solar panels. While its kickstand legs look similar to those of other budget folding panels, they are larger and sturdier. This panel is more wind-resistant than other folding models we tested, especially when you use stakes to secure the legs. It also has a zippered pouch for storing cables when you're not using them, which keeps things much tidier in a packed trunk. 
 The Jackery SolarSaga 200 is also very easy to set up. We had this panel upright and charging in 35 seconds. It has kickstand legs that deploy quickly, and the magnetic closure on the handle opens easily when you want it to, not when you don't. The charging cable has an 8 mm DC connector, which pairs perfectly with the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 models we used for testing. If you're trying to use this panel with a different power station brand, you'll likely need to buy a common adaptor. Some panels come with several adaptors so they can easily attach to any power station battery, but not this one. 
 The Grecell 200W Portable went from folded to charging in 31 seconds, the shortest time of any model. This panel also comes with MC4 power cables with four different connector types, so it can connect to any power station without requiring you to purchase the correct adaptor. However, after the testing period, the stitching on the canvas covering the panel is already beginning to separate. This makes us skeptical about how long it will last. 
 The Goal Zero Boulder Briefcase took longer to set up than most of the other folding panels we tested.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 The Anker Solix PS200 set up in 43 seconds, which is still quite fast, albeit not quite the fastest. But this panel has tons of other useful features. The kickstand legs have snap buttons to adjust the angle. Each leg has four different attachment points at 30, 40, 50, and 80 degrees. Since the legs are on the longer side, it takes a bit of maneuvering to keep them spread out when setting up with one person. But this also makes the panel more stable once you've set it up. It has MC4 connector cables, but they're shorter than most other panels. For long-term use, we recommend getting an extension cable.
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible and JJN Bifacial 200W are also notable in this category. They take much longer to set up than the folding models. The BougeRV takes 400 seconds, and the JJN 600 seconds. However, neither of these panels needs to be taken down once you've attached them to the roof of your vehicle, so technically the setup time is zero seconds after the initial setup. But, mounting these panels requires some hardware and mechanical know-how. So if you aren't looking to install a panel on your vehicle's roof, you should opt for a folding, portable solar panel. 
 The BougeRV Arch 200W Flexible requires no setup time once you've mounted it to the roof of your vehicle.   Credit: Sam Schild 
 Conclusion
 Choosing the right portable solar panel for your camping setup can feel daunting. Making the correct purchase can be the difference between a panel that lasts a long time and one that leaves you short on charge in the backcountry. Now that we've given you our take on the best large solar panels, hopefully you can make the right purchasing decision for your needs. 
 Hopefully, this guide brings you to beautiful places with plenty of power for all your tech.   Credit: Sam Schild

 What You Get (and Don't) Under $500
 At this price point, expect 250–300 Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, up to about 600W of AC output, and one to three AC outlets on most units (the DC-only Anker C300 DC has none). That's enough for phones, laptops, small camp lights, a CPAP machine overnight, or a mini fridge for several hours — but not a full home-backup load like a sump pump or window AC unit.
 The biggest trade-off versus pricier units isn't capacity — it's solar input . Budget units typically cap around 100–200W of solar charging, meaning a full recharge from panels alone takes most of a sunny day. If solar charging speed matters more than price, look at our camping guide for mid-tier units with faster solar input.
 All three picks below use LiFePO4 (LFP) battery chemistry rather than older NMC lithium — this matters because LiFePO4 cells handle roughly 2,500–3,500 charge cycles before dropping to 80% capacity, versus 500–1,000 for NMC. At a similar price, always prefer LiFePO4.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC: Why It Matters at the Budget Tier
 At the under-$500 price point, you'll find both LiFePO4 and older NMC lithium units. The temptation is to buy the cheaper NMC option and save a little upfront. Here is why that is usually a mistake:
 Cycle life is the biggest factor. A LiFePO4 unit rated for 3,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge will last 8+ years if you use it every weekend. An NMC unit rated for 500 cycles at the same DoD will be noticeably degraded after 1–2 years of regular use. Over the life of the product, the LiFePO4 unit's cost-per-cycle is dramatically lower even if the upfront price is slightly higher.
 Thermal stability matters for portable use. LiFePO4 chemistry is inherently more stable at high temperatures — it won't enter thermal runaway the way NMC can if damaged or exposed to extreme heat. For a generator that lives in a car trunk, camping tent, or sunny garage, that's a meaningful safety advantage.
 Storage behavior differs too. LiFePO4 batteries lose capacity much more slowly during long-term storage. If you buy a budget generator for emergency backup and only use it during power outages (potentially months apart), LiFePO4 will hold its charge and capacity far better than NMC without regular maintenance charging.
 The only scenario where NMC still makes sense at the budget tier is if you need the absolute lightest possible unit and are willing to replace it more often — but even then, the weight difference at the 250–300 Wh size is typically only a few ounces. All three of our picks below use LiFePO4, and we recommend you filter for that chemistry regardless of which unit you choose.
 Best Solar Panels to Pair with Budget Generators
 Budget solar generators typically accept 100–200W of solar input. That's enough for trickle-charging during a camping trip or topping off over a day, but not enough for a full recharge from empty in a few hours. Here's how to get the most out of solar charging on a budget unit:
 Match the brand's panel for best compatibility. Anker, Jackery, and EcoFlow all make 50–100W panels designed to pair with their budget units. These panels use proprietary connectors that work without adapters, and the folding suitcase design makes setup simple.
 A 100W panel is the sweet spot. A budget unit with 100W of solar input can fully recharge from empty in about 3–4 hours of direct sun (assuming 250–300 Wh capacity). That's fast enough to run devices at night and recharge during the day.
 Third-party panels work with the right adapter. If you already own generic solar panels (common 12V panels with MC4 connectors), you can buy an inexpensive adapter cable to connect them to most brand-name generators. Just make sure the voltage range is compatible — most budget units accept 12–28V input.
 Consider a bundled panel+generator kit. Many brands offer the generator with a compatible panel at a bundled price. If you know you'll want solar charging (and most camping users do), the bundle is usually a better value than buying separately.
 Even with a modest 50–100W panel, a budget solar generator becomes a sustainable off-grid power source for phones, tablets, a laptop, and camp lights — you just won't be running anything with a large motor or heating element for long.
 Realistic Use Cases for a Solar Generator Under $500
 A budget solar generator won't power your home during a multi-day outage or run a construction site. Here's what it will do well:
 Weekend camping trips: Phone charging, headlamps, a camp fan, a speaker, and camera batteries for 2–3 nights. With a 100W panel, fully self-sufficient off-grid.
 CPAP backup at a campsite or hotel: A 288 Wh unit runs a CPAP (without humidifier) for roughly 6–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep with margin.
 Emergency device charging during short outages: Keep phones, tablets, laptop, and router running for 1–2 days during a brief power outage. Enough to work from home, stay informed, and keep kids entertained.
 Car camping / road trip convenience: Charge devices without running your vehicle's engine or draining its starter battery. Some units double as a jump starter or have built-in LED lights for campsite illumination.
 Tailgating and outdoor events: Run a small speaker, phone charger, and a small portable fan for several hours — a big upgrade over disposable batteries and USB power banks.
 What it won't do: Run a full-size refrigerator for more than a few hours, power a sump pump or window AC unit, or keep your whole home running through a multi-day outage. For those scenarios, step up to our home backup guide for larger-capacity units.

 Is a solar generator under $500 worth it?

 What's the cheapest reliable solar generator?

Avoid no-name brands on Amazon with inflated capacity claims — they often exaggerate watt-hour ratings and use poor-quality cells.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC — does it matter at the budget tier? 
 Yes, significantly. LiFePO4 batteries last 2,500–3,500+ charge cycles versus 500–1,000 for NMC lithium. At a similar price, LiFePO4 is the better long-term value even though it's sometimes marginally heavier. All three of our picks use LiFePO4.
 Can a solar generator under $500 run a CPAP machine? 
 Yes. CPAP machines draw 30–60W (without humidifier), so a 288 Wh budget unit can run one for roughly 5–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep.  A 288 Wh unit will charge a smartphone roughly 20–25 times, run a 15W laptop for 15–18 hours, power a 40W camp fan for 6–7 hours, or run a mini cooler for 4–6 hours. For a CPAP without humidifier, expect one full night. Actual runtime depends on what you plug in and whether you're charging devices simultaneously.
 Can I add a solar panel to a budget generator later? 
 Yes, all three picks above have a dedicated solar input port. You can buy the generator now and add a compatible panel later when your budget allows. Just make sure the panel's voltage and connector type match the generator — check the specs before buying a panel, especially if mixing brands.
 How do budget solar generators compare to power banks? 
 A solar generator is essentially a very large power bank with built-in AC (wall-style) outlets. A typical portable power bank holds 20–30 Wh (enough for 4–6 phone charges) and only has USB outputs. A budget solar generator holds 250–300 Wh and usually has standard AC outlets (DC-only models like the Anker C300 DC are the exception), meaning it can power anything you'd plug into a wall — laptops, CPAP machines, fans, small appliances — not just USB devices.

But sifting through all the available options on the market — power stations that are lunchbox-sized to luggage-sized, solar panels that can pack in a backpack to multiple eight-foot long panels you chain together — can take a lot of time and effort. To help you choose the best solar generator for your purpose, we tested some of the most innovative models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Goal Zero, Bluetti, Anker, BioLite, Lion Energy, Ugreen, Vtoman, and more to see how they stacked up.

 How I Tested the Best Solar Generators
 There are two components to a solar generator: a solar panel and a power station. In my first and second rounds of testing of solar generators — in 2022 and 2023 — I focused on tandem testing to see how much power each pairing could produce, side-by-side, in the field. 
 An early test I ran of the best solar generators. Laura Lancaster 
 While this testing was valuable for learning about solar generators, and the issues that can arise out in the field, it didn’t provide sufficient granular information about the performance differences between the sola -generator components. So for my third round of testing I separated out the power stations and the solar panels and put them each through a series of rigorous tests. 
 Testing the Solar Panels
 One of many rounds or solar panel testing I conducted over the last two years. Laura Lancaster 
 In a solar generator setup, solar panels are what generate power. To determine how effective they were at doing just that, I tested 14 different solar panels both under clear skies and under clouds. This testing was conducted over the course of several years, with the same Anker SOLIX 100W panel serving as the control for each test. 
 ↓ Jump to Testing Results for Recommended Solar Panels 
 I also evaluated the panels on their portability and ease of use. Finally, I looked at their lowest operating temperature and their IP rating — a third-party test of water resistance and dust resistance. 
 Read the Full Story: The Best Portable Solar Panels 
 Testing the Power Stations
 Testing the max wattage potential of the power station component of the best solar generators. Laura Lancaster 
 If the solar panels are what is generating your power, the power station is what captures it, stores it, and releases the power when you need it. But the power station also uses some of that stored energy to power itself. I tested 9 power stations with the latest LiFePo4 battery chemistry on both a low draw (34 watts) and a high draw (380 watts) to see which was the most efficient at converting stored power to usable power. I also evaluated portability and ease of use. For this test, I started from scratch, calling in units from nine different manufacturers for testing in February 2024. Between June and September 2024, I additionally conducted long-term storage testing, to validate how much capacity users can expect to lose over time. 
 ↓ Jump to Testing Results for Recommended Power Stations 
 I also considered the maximum solar input of each power station as well as its lowest operating temperature and IP rating. 
 Read the Full Story: The Best Portable Power Stations 
 Choosing a Solar Generator Package
 While it is possible to mix and match solar panels and power stations, it can be a bit tricky. You need to make sure that the ports are compatible, as different brands use different connectors. You also need to make sure that the power station can handle the power input of the solar panel. For this story, I chose solar generators where the power station and solar panel components were made by the same company. 
 How I’m Assessing Price and Value
 As of 2025, I’m evaluating solar generator packages on their price and relative value. The challenge with this analysis is that, in this category, “list price” is essentially meaningless. More often than not, solar generator manufacturers will run so-called sales on their products, to create the illusion that you are getting an especially great deal if you jump now to pick up a unit. Sometimes, especially around Black Friday, this is true. Usually it’s not. It’s companies trying to manufacture the false impression among consumers that something is a “deal” so that they make an uninformed purchase. Don’t fall for it, especially not in a category that’s this pricey.

I determined this by looking at the average cost per usable watt hour from the units in the 1,000 Wh range in my test of the best portable power stations . This was $0.82 per watt hour. Next, I looked at the average cost per produced watt from the claimed 200W options in my test of the best portable solar panels. This was $2.84 per produced watt.

This can be a bit of a chore if you plan to swap out cords on a regular basis, but if you’re setting up a static off-grid system that you won’t be fiddling with too much, it has a nicer aesthetic.

Despite the petite size of the Anker SOLIX C1000, it’s a surprisingly powerful power station. It can handle a hearty solar input load, up to 600 watts. It can also put out 2400 watts at 120 volts, which will allow you to power most anything, from a fridge, to a CPAP machine, to a microwave.
 Testing the Anker SOLIX C1000 Solar Generator against a similarly sized setup from Lion Energy. Laura Lancaster 
 While Anker is boasting that this has an extremely fast turnover in the event of a power outage, which would theoretically allow you to keep critical systems going without a hitch, the reality is that the power it holds (1056Wh) and can generate at a time (200 watts) may not be enough to sustain you for a longer power outage. If there is medical equipment that is necessary for your or your loved’s one day-to-day survival, look into a larger power station with more solar input potential like the Anker SOLIX F2000. But if you’re looking for a unit that can keep everyone’s phones juiced with the option to turn on your coffee maker, then this one is hard to beat. 
 I had previously recommended pairing the Anker SOLIX C1000 with Anker’s 100-watt solar panel; however, they have made some changes to this model since I last tested it. The most noticeable change was the removal of the sundial feature, which is essential, in my experience, for maximizing the power output of a smaller unit. As such, I’m now recommending their larger 200W solar panel, described above in the recommendation for the best solar generator for RVs. While Anker’s 200W panel is more cumbersome than I would prefer, it will still provide plenty of power even when not optimally pointed toward the sun. Critically, even someone of a smaller stature can carry both the panel and the power station at the same time. If you’re interested in checking out the older model of the Anker SOLIX 100W, you can purchase a refurbished version of it on Amazon .

 In recent years, power station technology has advanced to Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePo4) , overtaking other lithium formulations, including lithium ion and NCM, for its longevity potential. These new formulations will last up to four times as long as older portable power stations. As such, I have removed power stations from the list that do not use this technology, including older models from Jackery and Anker, as well as the Goal Zero Yeti 1500X and the BioLite BaseCharge. I especially recommend avoiding power stations that utilize NCM chemistry, as one of the key components, cobalt, is associated with significant human rights atrocities in the Congo . 
 While I was tempted to include Goal Zero’s excellent weather-resistant Yeti 700X on this list, their solar panels are lacking. The Boulder panels, while cost effective, do not generate enough power relative to their size. The Nomad series does better, but neither the 100W panel nor the 200W panel have a handle on the carrying case. 
 While I was initially impressed with Lion Energy’s package of their Summit power station along with one of their 100-watt solar panels , further testing of the power station revealed that it is not effective at storing power long term. 
 I have also tested power stations and solar panels from Vtoman, Ugreen, and Dakota Lithium. Unfortunately, at this point, I have not found their performance to be on par with others in this category. See more in the results section for the best portable power stations and the best portable solar panels . 
 I tested the Zendure SuperBase V6400 paired with their 400W Solar Panel as part of my spring testing. This unit is massive: It comes saran-wrapped up on a pallet. While it does have wheels and a handle, that does not make it portable. It took a merciful delivery driver and myself an hour to get it up three floors to my home. This is not a realistic choice for overlanders or campers. Unless your rig has a ramp and a ton of excess of space I wouldn’t even consider it. Picture a 45 liter Yeti Tundra cooler that weighs 130 pounds.
 There were also problems with the Zendure SuperBase V6400 itself. The unit I had did not have functioning USB-C ports. I also noted that simply leaving the AC ports on overnight resulted in a 10 percent drop in the unit’s overall battery; surprising, given how many watt-hours it holds. Zendure confirmed that this is the expected functioning of the unit. One aesthetic note is that the latches for some of the port covers did not close correctly. The Zendure 400W Solar Panel was another story: It was surprisingly lightweight and easy to use given how much juice it generated. I only wish I could have paired it with a different power station.
 I strongly recommend heavily researching this unit before making a purchase, as you may be stuck with it. It requires original shipping materials (which I no longer had) and a pallet to return it. Local shipping companies were unable to supply one (at one point, Zendure suggested I purchase a pallet). I was unable to return this unit and it ultimately found its way to an acquaintance who works in IT. They’ve rigged it up to be the sole source of power for their bedroom, including servers and computers. They’re considering trying to use it as a source of power for their Tesla. If that sounds like what you’re hoping to do with your solar generator, then by all means give the Zendure package a look, but if you’re primarily looking for a unit for backup emergency power or for outdoors use, I’d give this one a pass.

 What Size Solar Generator Do I Need?
 If you’re looking to purchase a solar generator for the first time, the number of specifications to consider can be overwhelming. How many watt hours do you need? What is the difference between volts and amps? What’s a watt surge, anyway? Unless you’re already an electrician, it can be a steep learning curve.
 To help find a simpler answer to the question of what size solar generator you need for your home, I spoke to Ben Pattison, Director of Product Development at Goal Zero. As it turns out, the first thing that consumers should look for starts at home: “The primary question for someone to think about is what matters, what’s critical, and how long do I want to run it for,” said Pattison. “That’s really what’s gonna guide the decision-making for them.”
 Unfortunately, there isn’t a quick and easy way to estimate your energy needs. While it is theoretically possible to look at the meter for your house, most people only run critical systems during an emergency. And “critical” tends to be a pretty subjective term. For some people it could be their refrigerator and their space heater. For others, it could be a TV or other entertainment system. For instance, if you wanted to be able to run your refrigerator for a day (uses 67 watts per hour) and fully charge your lap top once per day (typically 51Wh), you’d need a power station that could had at least 1,659 watt-hour capacity. 
 You’ll also need to see what the maximum draw is for each of your electronics. While a refrigerator may use an average of 67 watts per hour, it doesn’t use that energy evenly: sometimes it will use 6 watts, sometimes it will surge and need 800 watts. Typically you can determine this number by multiplying the watt requirements by six (to guesstimate the needs), or by multiplying the amps and volts ratings together.
 At 115 volts, I can use three out of the five of the power stations in my test to power my fridge. Laura Lancaster 
 So the power station size you need will in large part depend on what your definition of “critical” is, with some individuals content to rough it as long as they can keep their phone charged and the space heater running while others may want something more substantial. For the former group, a best-in-class power station often suffices, as you can simply pick it up and move it to whichever room you currently need power in. But if you plan to power a larger chunk of your home, that quickly leads to a mess of power stations and extension cords. 
 Fortunately, Goal Zero is one of the solar generator companies that also sells solutions akin to gas generators. Their Haven 10 manual transfer switch gives you the option to back up 10 circuits in your home, transferring them over to power for your solar generator at the flip of a switch. However, this will (for most people) involve calling an electrician out to get it installed.
 While there are times when you know exactly when a blackout is going to happen and how long it’s going to last for (such as if your electrical utility is planning a rolling blackout), oftentimes people have no idea when a blackout is going to occur. That can make estimating your power needs as much art as science — during testing I saw the AC output regularly jump between 250 watts to over 1,000 watts depending on what appliances I was running. It’s also tough to know exactly how much you’ll be using each appliance in a power outage event — will you need to power a space heater during winter, or an air conditioner in the summer months?
 “That’s where solar becomes really important,” says Pattison. “Unfortunately, the sun isn’t consistent.” He suggests that people use the “rule of five” when determining how much solar they will need for their solar generator. For instance, if you’re purchasing a 4,000 watt hour power station, you’ll need 800 watts of solar to charge it up during the day. If it’s a 2,000 watt hour power station, you’ll need 400 watts of solar. However, if you know that the sun is even more limited at critical times of the year where you live, take that into consideration before making a final purchase. 
 Other Things to Consider Before Choosing the Best Solar Generator
 Budget
 Solar generators can be a pricey investment. Before you start looking at the various power stations and solar panels and package deals available, it’s important to know how much you are willing to spend. Underspending on a power station can result in inadequate power needs in the case of a power outage or while adventuring off grid. 
 Portability
 Power stations are often heavy, and solar panels can be unwieldy. Purchasing a larger unit than is necessary for your needs can reduce the utility of your overall setup — after all, if you hesitate to pull out your solar generator because of what a pain it is to set up, then it’s not doing you much good after all.
 Size
 While a single power station or a single solar panel may not take up much space, combined, they can start to add up. Consider how much storage space you have before making a final purchase. 
 FAQs
 Q: Are solar-powered generators worth the money? Solar-powered generators are expensive, especially if you are looking to power high-energy appliances, but for many people the peace of mind they bring makes them more than worth the money. Also, compared to gas-powered generators, solar-powered generators are quieter, lighter, and are free to recharge (no fuel costs), and so for many people are less expensive over the long run. The key is making sure you select a unit that can hold and generate enough power to run whatever you plan to plug in for an extended amount of time.
 Q: How do I choose a portable solar generator? While estimating your energy needs during a surprise blackout can be tough, if you are shopping for a solar generator for a car camping, RV, or overlanding setup, then you’ll be able to hone in more closely on your exact requirements. That’s because the manufacturers for these products assume that most individuals will be using them off the grid, and can provide reasonable estimates of how much juice you’ll need to power them for a set amount of time. 
 Q: Can a solar generator run a refrigerator? Yes, some solar generators can run refrigerators. There are two numbers that you need to line up when choosing the right solar generator for your needs: volts and watt-hours. First, look to see what the voltage requirements are of your refrigerator — you can typically find this on a sticker on the inside of your fridge.
Then choose a power station that can meet the voltage needs of your refrigerator. The watt-hours (Wh) essentially represent the size of the battery in your power station — the larger the battery, the longer it will power your fridge for, and the more it will cost. Typically, a 2,000Wh power station has enough juice to run your fridge for a day, but that depends on the power needs of your refrigerator, including the ambient air temperature and any add-ons running in the background. If you expect to have a solar generator powering a refrigerator for an extended period of time, choose larger, more powerful solar panels to pair with it, so that your refrigerator spends less time unplugged while the power station is recharging. 
 Q: Can a solar generator run an air conditioner? Yes, a solar generator paired with a power station can run an air conditioner. One thing you have to keep in mind is that the air conditioner’s power needs must match the power output of your power station. 
 Final Thoughts on the Best Solar Generators
 After testing the best solar generators for over a year — both individually and in tandem — it’s clear that the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 Pro (or 2000 Pro, depending on your power station needs) is one of the best setups available. While the Jackery combo can often be had on sale, if you’re looking to spend less money overall, the EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is a great option if you’re comfortable with a slightly more complicated setup. If you have a strong idea of exactly what your energy needs are, check out the sheer number of options offered by Goal Zero — panels that vary from 100W to 300W and power stations that go up to 6,000 watt-hours. Individuals and families on the go will appreciate the portability of the BioLite duo, while overlanders will benefit from the juice and portability of the Anker SOLIX F2000 power station and 531 Solar Panel.

Best Portable Power Stations Under $300 (2026): Tested and Ranked 
 J 
 Editor's Pick off-grid 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus
 8.7 /10 $279 
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus wins on LiFePO4 longevity, honest capacity numbers, and clean MPPT solar integration at $279.
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is the right buy for most people in this price class — 288Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, a genuine 100W MPPT solar input, and actual capacity numbers I verified against my Shelly EM energy clamp. This roundup is for campers, van dwellers, and homeowners building a small solar-charged backup kit for a laptop, CPAP machine, or 12V cooler when the grid goes down. I tested all five units on the same 100W portable panel and logged actual versus advertised solar charge times. Here is where each one lands.
 Quick Verdict 
 Winner — Jackery Explorer 300 Plus (~$279 standalone, ~$379 bundled with 100W panel): LiFePO4 longevity, honest capacity numbers, clean MPPT solar integration.
 Runner-Up — Anker Solix C300 (~$259): Better app monitoring, heavier body, thermal throttles under sustained high loads.
 Water Pick — EcoFlow River 3 (~$199 standalone, ~$249 bundled with panel): IP54 rated, lightest option, real 43Wh capacity gap versus the 288Wh units.
 Budget Pick — GENDOME Go 300 ($120): Half the price, measured capacity underperforms nameplate by 15%.
 Model Capacity AC Output Solar Input Battery Weight Price 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 100W MPPT LiFePO4 7.1 lbs ~$279 
 Anker Solix C300 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 100W MPPT LiFePO4 7.7 lbs ~$259 
 EcoFlow River 3 245Wh 300W / X-Boost to 600W 110W MPPT LFP 6.2 lbs ~$199 
 Litheli B288 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 80W LFP 7.4 lbs ~$209 
 GENDOME Go 300 288Wh 300W 60W Unconfirmed 7.9 lbs $120 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus
 Best for: solar-charged camping, overnight CPAP backup, small home emergency kits 
 The Explorer 300 Plus uses LiFePO4 chemistry at ~$279, and the upgrade from the old Explorer 300’s NMC cells matters more than the name change suggests. NMC rates for roughly 500 cycles before hitting 80% capacity. LFP is rated for 3,000 cycles — for a unit you charge weekly, that translates to 6 years of reliable use versus under 2. LFP also holds up better in cold conditions: where NMC can shed 20-25% capacity at 0°C, LFP typically loses 10-15%, which matters if you are camping in shoulder-season temperatures.
 In discharge testing, I pulled 280Wh before low-voltage cutoff — a 97% usable ratio against the 288Wh nameplate. That honesty is unusual at this price. I then paired the unit with a 100W monocrystalline panel at solar noon in June and logged input with my Shelly EM clamp. Full charge completed in 3 hours 22 minutes, versus the 3.5-hour advertised rate — honest numbers. At 70% cloud cover the same charge stretched past 7 hours as the MPPT controller de-rated proportionally. The unit accepts any MC4-terminated panel, not just Jackery’s own SolarSaga line, which matters if you already own a third-party panel.
 Pros: 
 LiFePO4 chemistry with 3,000-cycle warranty — longest longevity rating in this price tier
 280Wh measured usable capacity, 97% of the 288Wh nameplate
 USB-C 100W PD output charged a MacBook Pro from 20% to full in 87 minutes
 MPPT controller accepts third-party MC4 panels without adapters
 Cons: 
 AC inverter fan activates audibly above approximately 50W load — noticeable in a quiet tent at night
 No IP rating — splash exposure is a real risk in rain or on a boat
 Specific failure found: Under a 65W compressor cooler load, the internal wattage display consistently under-read by 7-8% compared to my Shelly clamp. Fine for casual use; do not rely on it for precise energy budgeting across a multi-day trip.
 Score: 8.7/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Anker Solix C300
 Best for: Anker ecosystem users and camp setups that benefit from granular monitoring 
 The Solix C300 matches the Jackery almost spec-for-spec at ~$259 — 288Wh, 300W output, LiFePO4, 100W MPPT solar input. The real differentiator is software: the Solix app refreshes at 1-second intervals and surfaces detailed charge and discharge curves that Jackery’s interface does not offer. If you want to track exactly how much a 100W panel is delivering versus what the station is consuming, this is the better tool. The built-in LED strip is also genuinely useful at camp — one press cycles through three brightness levels with enough spread to light a 4-person tent interior, not the token flashlight gimmick you see on cheaper units.
 Pros: 
 Solix app: 1-second refresh intervals, detailed charge history — best software integration in this roundup
 LiFePO4 3,000-cycle rating matches the Explorer 300 Plus
 Built-in LED with practical brightness range for tent use
 Anker warranty service response track record is faster than most competitors in this category
 Cons: 
 7.7 lbs versus Jackery’s 7.1 — 0.6 lbs matters over a full-day pack carry
 AC outlet placement on the unit’s short side creates an awkward cable hang when set flat on a table
 Specific failure found: Running a 480W-rated appliance triggered thermal throttling after 4 minutes and shut the load off mid-cycle. I ran the same appliance on the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus through a full 7-minute cycle without throttling. If you plan to use this with a high-draw appliance, test before you rely on it in the field.
 Score: 8.2/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 EcoFlow River 3
 Best for: kayakers, beach camping, and anywhere splash or rain exposure is likely 
 The River 3 enters at ~$199, and its headline spec is real: IP54 dust and splash resistance . No other unit in this roundup offers any water protection. If your use case involves boats, beach days, or Pacific Northwest camping where afternoon rain is routine, that rating justifies the 43Wh capacity gap versus the 288Wh units above. EcoFlow’s X-Boost technology lets the 300W inverter run appliances rated up to 600W by limiting draw during the off-peak portions of a load cycle — I tested it with a 500W blender and it completed the task, with noticeably longer blend times than rated.
 Pros: 
 IP54 water resistance — the only protected unit in this roundup under $300
 Lightest at 6.2 lbs — meaningful over a long carry
 110W MPPT solar ceiling is slightly above Jackery’s 100W
 X-Boost expands effective appliance compatibility past the inverter’s continuous rating
 Cons: 
 245Wh is a real 43Wh gap versus 288Wh competitors — relevant for overnight CPAP or multi-day off-grid use without a solar recharge in between
 The AC outlet cover is a rubber friction-fit flap that loosens noticeably after dozens of plug and unplug cycles
 Specific failure found: The EcoFlow app rounds solar input to the nearest 10W and updates every 3 seconds. With my panel producing 87W measured on the Shelly clamp, the app alternated between 80W and 90W on the display — making actual MPPT efficiency tracking impossible without an external meter.
 Score: 7.8/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Litheli B288
 Best for: buyers who need 288Wh capacity and catch a sale below $170 
 The B288 checks the core boxes at ~$209 — 288Wh, LFP battery chemistry, 300W output. The concrete constraint is the 80W maximum solar input. With any standard 100W portable panel in full sun, you are capped at 80W input, leaving 20W unused in every peak sun hour. That adds 35-40 minutes to a full charge cycle compared to the Jackery or EcoFlow and means you never actually utilize the panel you likely own or will buy.
 Pros: 
 Full 288Wh LFP capacity at a $70 discount versus the Jackery
 Handles standard CPAP and laptop loads reliably
 Compact form factor, comfortable to carry one-handed
 Cons: 
 80W solar input ceiling is a structural constraint when paired with the most common portable panel size on the market
 Thinner warranty service infrastructure than Jackery or EcoFlow — fewer service locations, slower response in my experience
 Specific failure found: The 12V DC output port drew a consistent 5W phantom load when nothing was connected — measured over 48 hours of idle monitoring with my Shelly clamp. That is roughly 3.6Wh of wasted standby drain every day you leave the unit plugged into a 12V outlet without using it.
 Score: 7.1/10 
 GENDOME Go 300
 Best for: buyers with a hard $120 ceiling who go in with clear expectations 
 At $120, the GENDOME Go 300 is half the Jackery’s price. That gap reflects real differences. Discharge testing hit low-voltage cutoff at 246Wh — an 85% usable ratio against the 288Wh nameplate, compared to the Jackery’s 97%. The 60W solar input ceiling means a 100W panel sits throttled at peak output; you lose 40W of available charging capacity in every peak sun hour. GENDOME does not publish cell chemistry publicly, and my measured discharge curve is consistent with NMC behavior rather than LFP — a steeper discharge slope at low state of charge and faster early-cycle capacity loss than LFP would produce.
 Pros: 
 $120 — lowest price for a 300W-class unit from any recognizable brand in this roundup
 Handles USB phone and tablet charging reliably
 Light enough for minimalist day hiking where heavy charging is not expected
 Cons: 
 Measured usable capacity of approximately 246Wh is 15% below the 288Wh nameplate claim
 No verifiable cell chemistry documentation, cycle life rating, or UL/CE certification published
 Specific failure found: After 90 charge cycles over three months, I measured 228Wh at full charge — an 11% capacity loss from baseline. Jackery and EcoFlow LFP units show under 3% loss over the same cycle count. If the chemistry is NMC as the discharge curve suggests, expect continued faster-than-rated long-term degradation.
 Score: 6.4/10 
 The Verdict
 For most buyers, the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus at ~$279 is the correct answer . LiFePO4 gives you 3,000 cycles before meaningful capacity loss, the MPPT input works cleanly with any standard 100W portable panel, and the actual capacity numbers are honest. If you camp weekly and rely on this for a CPAP or laptop over multiple seasons, the chemistry gap between the Jackery and the GENDOME alone justifies the price difference within two years of use.
 If water exposure is your primary risk , buy the EcoFlow River 3 at ~$199. IP54 is the correct engineering tradeoff for boat and beach use — the 43Wh gap matters far less than not destroying a station you depend on.
 Already in the Anker ecosystem? The Solix C300 at ~$259 adds genuine app monitoring depth. Test your highest-wattage appliance before trusting it in the field — the thermal throttling behavior is a real limitation for high-draw loads.
 Hard $120 ceiling? The GENDOME Go 300 will charge phones and laptops. Plan for the 15% capacity shortfall, the 60W solar input constraint, and faster long-term degradation than any LFP unit in this class.
 If you are pairing a portable station with a whole-home solar installation, compare quotes on EnergySage before committing — a properly sized home system changes what portable backup you actually need.
 FAQ
 Will a 300Wh power station run my CPAP all night? 
 A standard CPAP at 7-10cm pressure draws 30-45W. At 40W average, 288Wh gets you 6.5-7 hours — enough for most nights without humidification. Enable the humidifier and draw climbs to 60-70W, cutting runtime to 4-4.5 hours. If you run humidification nightly, a DC-mode CPAP adapter bypasses the inverter and cuts power draw by about 30%, buying back 1.5-2 hours of runtime.
 How do I pair one of these with a solar panel for off-grid camping? 
 A 100W monocrystalline panel at peak output delivers 85-95W to the unit after MPPT conversion losses. Over 5 peak sun hours, that is 425-475Wh of generation — enough to fully recharge any unit here and simultaneously power a device. I carry the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus with a 100W panel on cabin weekends and typically arrive with the station already at 100% from panel charging during the drive.
 Does the federal solar tax credit apply to portable power stations? 
 No. The Section 25D residential Investment Tax Credit expired December 31, 2025. Portable stations were never covered as standalone purchases under 25D — only home battery systems integrated with a solar installation qualified. There is no federal credit pathway for portable units purchased in 2026. State-level incentives like California’s SGIP also do not extend to portable equipment.
 Are no-name brands like GENDOME safe to use indoors or in a vehicle? 
 The main risk with unverified brands is battery management system quality. A weak BMS can fail to prevent overcharge, overdischarge, or thermal runaway events. Reputable brands publish cell chemistry, cycle ratings, and third-party safety certifications. GENDOME’s listing discloses none of these clearly. I would not use a unit with unverified chemistry inside a vehicle or near sleeping areas — the risk-to-savings ratio does not favor it.
